﴿with the Lord of mankind﴾, that is, the Owner of their affairs and the one who nurtures them by bestowing what benefits them and averting what harms them. His command to do so is among the signs of the generous promise of refuge without doubt. Some eminent scholars, in explaining the reason for the specification, restricted it to seeking refuge here from the evil that particularly affects human souls, which is the whispering (*waswasa*), as He said: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer﴾. This was criticized, after reflection, for falling short of fulfilling the station's due, since the evil of the whisperer affects bodies as well as souls. There is something in this which we will, God willing, point out. This researcher chose in this matter that, since seeking refuge in what preceded was from the evil of everything, the Lord was attributed to everything, that is, on the basis of the generality of "the daybreak." And since here it is from the evil of the whisperer, it was not attributed to everything. The consideration of the preceding surah required attribution to the whisperer, but it was not attributed to him, in order to lower his rank from being attributed to the Lord, and rather it was attributed to the one seeking refuge. In this lowering there is a symbol of the promise of refuge, and this is what gives this matter a share in fulfilling the station's due. It may be said that in the attribution of the Lord to mankind at the end of a surah of His Book there is a reminder of the first covenant, a matter they knew in the world of atoms, and on which He took from them a pledge to acknowledge Him afterward, as His words indicate: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their backs, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes"﴾, and so on. So in this there is an encouragement to seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer, lest the matter of that covenant be defiled. In it there is also a symbol of the generous promise of refuge.

Al-Qadi said that in this glorious composition there is an indication of the stages of the observer who turns toward knowing his Creator. He first knows, through the apparent and hidden blessings he sees upon himself, that he has a Lord. Then he penetrates deeper into contemplation until he realizes that He, glory be to Him, is independent of all things, and that the essence of everything belongs to Him and the ends of its affairs are from Him. So He is the true King. Then one is guided by Him to the conclusion that He alone deserves worship. This is included among the customary ways of seeking refuge, treating difference of attributes as difference of essences. For the habit of one who is struck by a worry is to raise his matter to his master and nurturer, such as his parents. If he cannot remove it through them, he raises it to his king and ruler. If that does not remove his injustice, he complains to the King of kings, to whom complaints and refuge belong. In this there is an indication of the magnitude of the calamity from which refuge is sought.

Ibn Sina has here a discourse from which pens shrink, as is not hidden from one who has come across it and who had some slight acquaintance with the purified Sharia.

The repetition of the genitive attribution ("mankind") is for greater disclosure, confirmation, and honoring through attribution. It has been said: there is no repetition, for it is possible that by the general term is meant some of its members. So the first "mankind" means the fetuses and children who need nurture; the second means the middle-aged and the young, since they are the ones who need someone to govern them; and the third means the elderly devoted to worship, who turn toward God, exalted is He. However, on what is in it, this view is far-fetched, given the rule that repeating a noun in the definite form (ma'rifa) is the usual practice, even if it is mostly so.

According to al-Zamakhshari, *al-waswās* is a noun of action (*ism maṣdar*) meaning *al-waswasa* (the whispering). The verbal noun is with a kasra and refers to the sound of jewelry and to a hidden murmur. Then it was used for a bad thought, and here it is meant as Satan, named by his action for emphasis, as if he exhaled the whispering or the speech. Or the expression is elliptical, meaning "the one of the whisperings" (*dhī al-waswās*). Some grammarians of Arabic said: *faʿlala* has two forms: a sound one like *daḥraja* (to roll), and a biliteral doubled one like *ṣalṣala* (to ring). Both have regular verbal nouns: *faʿlala* and *fiʿlāl* with a kasra, which is more analogous. The fatha is irregular, but it has become common in doubled forms like *tamtām* (stammerer) and *fa'fa'a* (stammering). It may serve for emphasis, like *faʿʿāl* in triliterals, as they said *waṭwāṭ* for a weak man and *thartār* for one who talks much. The truth is that it is an adjective, and what is in the noble verse should be understood as such, without the need for metaphor or for ellipsis of a noun. What relates to this topic has already been mentioned in Surat al-Zalzala, so remember it, for there is nothing old in what is well known.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended is seeking refuge from the evil of the whisperer as such, as a whisperer, and this ultimately amounts to seeking refuge from the evil of his whispering. It has also been said that what is intended is seeking refuge from all of his evils. For this reason it was said "from the evil of the whisperer," and it was not said "from the whispering of the whisperer." It has been said: according to this, the view that his evil reaches the body as it reaches the soul is more apparent than on the plain reading. And among his evils it is counted that, as in Sahih al-Bukhari, he "ties three knots on the nape of the servant's neck when he sleeps," the meaning of which is to prevent him from waking. The inclusion of this under bodily evil is obscure. Some have counted among his evils the derangement (*takhabbut*) that afflicts a person, which, according to the people of the Sunna, may come from his touch, as was mentioned in its place.

His words, ﴿the one who withdraws﴾, are an intensive form (*ṣīgha mubālagha*) or a relative adjective, meaning: the one whose habit is to withdraw and draw back when a person remembers his Lord, mighty and majestic is He.

Al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtāra*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "No child is born except that the whisperer is upon his heart. When he understands and remembers God, exalted is He, he withdraws. When he becomes heedless, he whispers." According to what is related from Qatada, he has a snout like the snout of a dog, and it is said that his head is like the head of a snake.

Ibn Shahin narrated from Anas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed the whisperer has a snout like the beak of a bird. When the son of Adam becomes heedless, he places that beak in the ear of the heart and whispers. If he remembers God, exalted is He, he recoils and withdraws. Therefore he is called the whisperer who withdraws.'"

Rather, it is in the manner of worship (*maʿbūdiyya*), founded upon divinity (*ulūhiyya*), which requires complete power over disposing of them in every way: giving life, causing death, bringing into existence, and annihilating. The apposition (*badaliyya*) has also been permitted, and you know that there is no rational impediment to it. Then, what is here, although it is not an inert noun, is in the same ruling. Perhaps eloquence called for choosing this and for specifying the attribution to "mankind," even though the whole world is included under His lordship, sovereignty, and divinity, in order to guide to the method of seeking refuge in its true sense, by being granted refuge. For the servant who seeks refuge, invoking his Lord and attributing himself to Him through lordship, ownership, and servitude, within a category that is one of its members, is among the causes of increased mercy and compassion. His command to do so is among the signs of the generous promise of refuge without doubt. Also, because the thing sought refuge from is the evil of Satan, known for his enmity toward them, the explicit mention of their being included under His worship and sovereignty is a symbol of their deliverance from Satan's dominion and his power over them, as His words indicate: ﴿Indeed, My servants, over them you have no authority﴾.

Some eminent scholars, in explaining the reason for the specification, restricted it to seeking refuge here from the evil that particularly affects human souls, which is the whispering (*waswasa*), as He said: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer﴾. This was criticized, after reflection, for falling short of fulfilling the station's due, since the evil of the whisperer affects bodies as well as souls. There is something in this which we will, God willing, point out. This researcher chose in this matter that, since seeking refuge in what preceded was from the evil of everything, the Lord was attributed to everything, that is, on the basis of the generality of "the daybreak." And since here it is from the evil of the whisperer, it was not attributed to everything. The consideration of the preceding surah required attribution to the whisperer, but it was not attributed to him, in order to lower his rank from being attributed to the Lord, and rather it was attributed to the one seeking refuge. In this lowering there is a symbol of the promise of refuge, and this is what gives this matter a share in fulfilling the station's due. It may be said that in the attribution of the Lord to mankind at the end of a surah of His Book there is a reminder of the first covenant, a matter they knew in the world of atoms, and on which He took from them a pledge to acknowledge Him afterward, as His words indicate: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their backs, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes"﴾, and so on. So in this there is an encouragement to seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer, lest the matter of that covenant be defiled. In it there is also a symbol of the generous promise of refuge.

Al-Qadi said that in this glorious composition there is an indication of the stages of the observer who turns toward knowing his Creator. He first knows, through the apparent and hidden blessings he sees upon himself, that he has a Lord. Then he penetrates deeper into contemplation until he realizes that He, glory be to Him, is independent of all things, and that the essence of everything belongs to Him and the ends of its affairs are from Him. So He is the true King. Then one is guided by Him to the conclusion that He alone deserves worship. This is included among the customary ways of seeking refuge, treating difference of attributes as difference of essences. For the habit of one who is struck by a worry is to raise his matter to his master and nurturer, such as his parents. If he cannot remove it through them, he raises it to his king and ruler. If that does not remove his injustice, he complains to the King of kings, to whom complaints and refuge belong. In this there is an indication of the magnitude of the calamity from which refuge is sought.

Ibn Sina has here a discourse from which pens shrink, as is not hidden from one who has come across it and who had some slight acquaintance with the purified Sharia.

The repetition of the genitive attribution ("mankind") is for greater disclosure, confirmation, and honoring through attribution. It has been said: there is no repetition, for it is possible that by the general term is meant some of its members. So the first "mankind" means the fetuses and children who need nurture; the second means the middle-aged and the young, since they are the ones who need someone to govern them; and the third means the elderly devoted to worship, who turn toward God, exalted is He. However, on what is in it, this view is far-fetched, given the rule that repeating a noun in the definite form (ma'rifa) is the usual practice, even if it is mostly so.

According to al-Zamakhshari, *al-waswās* is a noun of action (*ism maṣdar*) meaning *al-waswasa* (the whispering). The verbal noun is with a kasra and refers to the sound of jewelry and to a hidden murmur. Then it was used for a bad thought, and here it is meant as Satan, named by his action for emphasis, as if he exhaled the whispering or the speech. Or the expression is elliptical, meaning "the one of the whisperings" (*dhī al-waswās*). Some grammarians of Arabic said: *faʿlala* has two forms: a sound one like *daḥraja* (to roll), and a biliteral doubled one like *ṣalṣala* (to ring). Both have regular verbal nouns: *faʿlala* and *fiʿlāl* with a kasra, which is more analogous. The fatha is irregular, but it has become common in doubled forms like *tamtām* (stammerer) and *fa'fa'a* (stammering). It may serve for emphasis, like *faʿʿāl* in triliterals, as they said *waṭwāṭ* for a weak man and *thartār* for one who talks much. The truth is that it is an adjective, and what is in the noble verse should be understood as such, without the need for metaphor or for ellipsis of a noun. What relates to this topic has already been mentioned in Surat al-Zalzala, so remember it, for there is nothing old in what is well known.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended is seeking refuge from the evil of the whisperer as such, as a whisperer, and this ultimately amounts to seeking refuge from the evil of his whispering. It has also been said that what is intended is seeking refuge from all of his evils. For this reason it was said "from the evil of the whisperer," and it was not said "from the whispering of the whisperer." It has been said: according to this, the view that his evil reaches the body as it reaches the soul is more apparent than on the plain reading. And among his evils it is counted that, as in Sahih al-Bukhari, he "ties three knots on the nape of the servant's neck when he sleeps," the meaning of which is to prevent him from waking. The inclusion of this under bodily evil is obscure. Some have counted among his evils the derangement (*takhabbut*) that afflicts a person, which, according to the people of the Sunna, may come from his touch, as was mentioned in its place.

His words, ﴿the one who withdraws﴾, are an intensive form (*ṣīgha mubālagha*) or a relative adjective, meaning: the one whose habit is to withdraw and draw back when a person remembers his Lord, mighty and majestic is He.

Al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtāra*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "No child is born except that the whisperer is upon his heart. When he understands and remembers God, exalted is He, he withdraws. When he becomes heedless, he whispers." According to what is related from Qatada, he has a snout like the snout of a dog, and it is said that his head is like the head of a snake.

Ibn Shahin narrated from Anas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed the whisperer has a snout like the beak of a bird. When the son of Adam becomes heedless, he places that beak in the ear of the heart and whispers. If he remembers God, exalted is He, he recoils and withdraws. Therefore he is called the whisperer who withdraws.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 114, verse 5:

﴿Who whispers into the breasts of mankind﴾. It has been said that what is meant is their hearts, by way of metaphor (majaz). Some of them said: Indeed, Satan enters the chest (ṣadr), which is in the position of the vestibule (dihliz), and from there he casts into it what he wishes to cast into the heart, and he conveys it to the heart. There is no rational obstacle (māni') to his entering the inner body of the human being, and the revealed text (al-sam') has come with this, as you have heard. So it is obligatory to accept it and to believe in it. Among the evidence for this is the hadith: "Indeed, Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows."

Among people there are those who understood it as a figurative expression (tamthil) and said that the verse does not imply entry, as the explanation that follows indicates. Ibn Sina said: The whisperer (al-waswās) is the faculty that produces the whispering, namely the imaginative faculty (al-quwwa al-mutakhayyila), insofar as it is employed by the animal soul (al-nafs al-hayawāniyya). Then its movement is in the opposite direction, because the soul is oriented toward the separate principles (al-mabādi' al-mufāriqa). So when the imaginative faculty is occupied only with matter and its attachments, that faculty recedes (takhnis), that is, it moves in the opposite direction and draws the human soul toward the opposite. For this reason it is called "the one who recedes" (al-khannās). Similar to this is what has been said: that it is the estimative faculty (al-quwwa al-wahmiyya), which assists the intellect in the premises, and when the matter reaches the conclusion it recedes and begins to whisper to it and cast doubt into it. It is not hidden that interpreting the words of God Most High by such things is among the evil of the whispering, the one who recedes.

Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) mentioned the latter only as an analogy (ʿalā sabīl al-tanẓīr), not as a figurative interpretation or an explanation, on the basis of good opinion of him.

The place of the relative pronoun (maḥall al-mawṣūl) is either genitive, as a qualifier (waṣf), or nominative or accusative, as a reproach or abuse (dhamm wa-shatm). It is good for the reader to pause (yaqif) on ﴿al-khannās﴾ according to either of these two possibilities. As for the first, al-Kawashi (al-Kawāshī) stated that pausing is not permissible, and al-Tibi (al-Ṭībī) criticized this, saying that denying its permissibility is open to question because of the verse-ending (fāṣila). In al-Kashf it is stated that if it is a qualifier, then the goodness of the pause is not accepted, except in one way: that the general rule of good pausing (al-waqf al-ḥasan) includes its like in a specific verse-ending.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 114, verse 6:**

﴿from among the jinn and mankind﴾ is an explanation of "the one who whispers," indicating that he is of two kinds: a jinn and a human, as God the Exalted says: ﴿Satans from among mankind and the jinn﴾. Or it may be connected to "whispers," with "min" (from) denoting the starting point, meaning: he whispers in their breasts from the direction of the jinn, such as casting into a person's heart, from their direction, that they benefit and harm, and from the direction of mankind, such as casting into his heart, from their direction, the notion of astrologers and soothsayers, and that they know the unseen. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿whispers﴾, and an apposition (badal) to God's words ﴿from the evil﴾, by repeating the preposition and supposing an omitted noun, and an apposition to "the whisperer" on the basis that "min" is partitive. Al-Farra' and a group said: it is an explanation of "mankind," on the basis that it is also applied to the jinn, so it is said, as was reported from al-Kalbi: "men of the jinn" (nas min al-jinn), just as it is said: "a band and men of them" (nafar wa rijal minhum). But in this there is that what is known among people is the opposite of it, together with what there is in that of resemblance to making a part of a thing a counterpart to it, and the like of this does not suit the eloquence of the Qur'an, even if its soundness is granted. It has also been objected that it necessarily entails the claim that Satan whispers in the breasts of the jinn just as he whispers in the breasts of humans, and no proof has been established for this. And it is not permissible to make the verse a proof for what is not hidden. Closer to it, according to what has been said, is that "mankind" (al-nas) is meant as "the forgetful" (al-nasi), with the ya', like the reading of some of them: "from where the people pour forth" (min haythu afada al-nasi), with a kasra, and the dropping of the ya' is made like its dropping in God's words: ﴿the day the caller calls﴾. Then it is explained by "the jinn and mankind," for each individual of the two groups is afflicted with forgetting God's right, except one whom the intercessions of His protection overtake and the vastness of His mercy embraces. May God make us among those who obtain the fullest share of His protection, and whose Lord, from His mercy, suffices him abundantly.

Then it has been said: the letters of this surah, without repetition, are twenty-two letters, and likewise the letters of al-Fatiha; and that corresponds to the number of years in which the Qur'an was revealed, so let it be examined. And after the matter has been found as mentioned, it is not hidden that the number of years of revelation being twenty-two is the view of some. The well-known view is that they are twenty-three, due to the Mighty. Of the same kind of cipher is what has been said: that the first of its letters is the bá' and its last is the sín, as if it were said "bas," meaning "enough"; so in it is an indication that it is sufficient in place of anything else. And it alludes to God's words: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾. Some Persians have versified this, saying:

*The beginning and end of the Qur'an, what came in: the bá' and the sín, that is, in both worlds, our guide is the Qur'an, enough (bas).*

Of such ciphers there are many, but it has been said: it is not appropriate to say that this is what God, Mighty and Majestic, intends. Yes, He, Mighty and Majestic, has guided in this surah to seeking help from Him, exalted is His majesty, just as He guided to it in al-Fatiha. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that what He, exalted, intends, on the view that the arrangement of the surahs is by His revelation, glorified is He, from concluding His noble Book with seeking refuge in Him from the evil of the whisperer, is an indication, as in al-Fatiha, to the exalted status of piety, and an allusion to its being the foundation of the whole matter, and that through it a good end is attained. So glorified is He, a King Majestic; how sublime is His word! And to God belongs the excellence of the Revelation, how fine is its opening and its closing!

Now then, this—and praise be to God—is the interpretation of my dream of before, which my Lord made true; so He made me happy, and to Him is thanks, by granting success in the interpretation of His mighty Book, which does not humiliate whoever takes refuge in it, nor does he become wretched. So since You have granted me success, O my God, in interpreting its expression, and granted me success in what You willed of its hidden allusion, then make me, O my Lord, among those who hold fast to its firm rope, and grasp its most secure handle, and take refuge from the ambiguous things in the fortress of its stronghold, and shade themselves in the shadows of its most complete cave. Protect me by it from the whisperings of Satan and his plots, and from being entangled in the net of his deception and his snares. Make it a means for me to the most noble stations of honor, and a ladder by which I ascend to the place of safety. For how long, O my God, have its verses kept me awake, until sleep's drowsiness nodded on my head, so I did not awaken except that I had been struck by the edges of the pages of a surah having bracelets. And how many, how many times, O my Master, its expressions have carried me along, until the claim was realized for me: "At dawn the people praise the night journey." I was not aware until I had wrapped myself in the drowsy eyes of the darkness, from the excess of the wrapper of the gazelle of dawn with a veil. And I did not cease blackening pages in writing down what You poured upon me, until my life's copy was whitened by gray hair, and the gaze renewed by the staring of eyes at what was poured upon me of the shaykhs, until the cloak of my youth wore out. This is along with what I have suffered from a treacherous friend, and a harsh, unjust great one, and a tyrannical time, and clouds whose rain is sorrows, and matters in which You, O my God, know best, and there was none for me in them besides You who would show mercy. Most of that, O my God, was when You qualified me to serve Your Book, and bestowed upon me without limit the favor of searching the repositories of Your address. So suffice me, O God, by its sanctity, from the burden of the disgrace of the servants, and grant me security on the Day of Return. Protect me by Your kindness, protect me by Your blessing, and grant me success in what is best, employ me in what is most pleasing, and guide me on the most excellent path. Provide me with mounts of guidance, and provide me with enduring piety. Set right my offspring, and by them let me attain my wish, and make them learned and acting scholars, and guided guides. Be for me and for them in all matters, protect me and protect them from the trials of the house of delusion. O God, strengthen Your vicegerent in Your creation, and grant him success, by the sanctity of Your speech, in exalting Your word. And send blessings and peace upon the spirit of the meanings of all possibilities without restriction, and the spirit of the meanings of the hearts of the believing men and women, in all the horizons, and upon his family and companions, and everyone who followed the ways of his Sunnah, and pursued it, and who said, in the shade of the cool shadow of his Shari'ah, saying: "That is enough for me, and sufficient."

The handing over of the pen coincided with its bowing and prostration, in the darkness of the blackness of ink, and its lying down in the house of the inkwell, after its standing on the leg of service to the Book of the Lord of the servants, on the night of Tuesday, four days having passed in the month of Rabi' al-Akhir in the year one thousand two hundred and sixty-seven, from the Hijra of the master of the first and the last, may God the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. Its chronogram is: "My tafsir, Ruh al-Ma'ani, was completed, and praise be to God, outwardly and inwardly, and to Him, glorified is He, is thanks, first and last."
